p: The Hebrew title is the first word, the cry that opens a funeral song.
b: 'Eikhah, "How!", is the first word of chapters 1, 2 and 4 (and of 4:2), and it is the Hebrew title of the book. It is the cry that opens a dirge: the shorter form 'eikh begins David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:19, 25, 27) and the lament over Moab (Jeremiah 48:17), and 'eikhah opens Isaiah's lament over the faithful city (Isaiah 1:21). It asks no question. It says that something unthinkable has happened. The Talmud calls the book Qinot, "Laments" (Bava Batra 14b). The Greek title is Threnoi and the Latin Threni, "Dirges", and Jerome's Vulgate also uses Lamentationes, from which the English name comes.

t: The alphabet behind the first words
p: Chapters 1, 2 and 4 give each verse the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, alef to tav.
b: In Hebrew, verse 1 begins with alef, verse 2 with bet, verse 3 with gimel, and so on to tav at verse 22. English cannot copy this without bending the meaning, so the Plain English Translation does not try. It keeps a matching first letter only where it falls out by itself: 1:3 "Gone" happens to match gimel (galetah), and that is chance, not design. The chapter page lists all 22 letters with the Hebrew first word of each verse. Chapter 5 also has 22 verses but no alphabet (see 5:1). The same form appears in Psalm 119, Proverbs 31:10-31 and Nahum 1:2-8. One view takes the whole alphabet, alef to tav, as completeness: saying everything, from first letter to last, when everything has fallen apart. See also the topic page on alphabet poems.

p: The Hebrew names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition says Jeremiah; most modern scholars doubt it.
b: Tradition. The Talmud says Jeremiah wrote his book, the Book of Kings and Lamentations (Bava Batra 15a). Second Chronicles 35:25 says Jeremiah made a lament for Josiah, kept in "the Laments", and Josephus (Antiquities 10.5.1) says it still existed in his day. The Greek Bible opens with a prose preface that the Hebrew lacks: "And it happened, after Israel was taken captive and Jerusalem laid waste, that Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented this lament over Jerusalem, and said..." (translated here from Swete's printed text). The Clementine Vulgate has the same preface as a prologue before the first letter, but ends it differently: "...sighing and wailing in bitterness of spirit, he said". The Hebrew has no preface. Modern scholarship. Hillers, Berlin, Provan and Dobbs-Allsopp deny Jeremiah: the poems mourn the fallen king (4:20) where Jeremiah told Judah to submit, and chapter 3's trust differs from his harsher oracles. Some think chapters 1, 2 and 4 are eyewitness work, chapter 3 another poet's, chapter 5 later; others think one poet. Nearly all date the poems within a generation of 586 BC. The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew only.

a: She who was great among the nations
p: The Hebrew lines are long then short; English cannot keep that beat, so the Plain English Translation keeps the line breaks.
b: Most lines in chapters 1 to 4 are a longer line followed by a shorter one, about three beats and then two. Karl Budde named this the qinah ("lament") measure and Delbert Hillers described it for Lamentations: the second line seems to fall short of the first, like a sob or a limp. English words do not stress in the same way, so no English version keeps it. The Plain English Translation keeps what it can: three short lines to each verse in chapters 1 and 2, one line in chapter 3, two in chapters 4 and 5, so a reader can see the shape even if the beat is lost.

p: Jerusalem is a woman whose husband is gone; a widow had no one to protect her.
b: The poet speaks of the city as a woman. A widow, especially one with no grown sons, had no income and no protector in Israel (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18). Jerusalem is "like" a widow, not a widow: the king lives, though captured (4:20), and Isaiah can promise that Zion will forget the shame of her widowhood (Isaiah 54:4). The picture of a bereft woman runs through the whole book: a mother who has lost children (1:5, 16), an abandoned wife (1:2), a woman stripped and shamed (1:8-10).

p: The Hebrew word is the royal labor gang, the draft of free people for building work.
b: Mas was the conscripted labor of free people, as Solomon drafted Israelites to cut timber and build (1 Kings 5:13) and as conquered peoples were made to work (Genesis 49:15; 1 Kings 9:21). The princess has become a worker in the labor gang: the greatest of the provinces is now someone else's property.

p: This sentence returns like a refrain: 1:2, 9, 16, 17, 21. Isaiah 40:1 is its answer.
b: 'En lah menachem is the book's refrain: "she has no one to comfort her" (1:2, 9, 17), "no one to comfort me" (1:21), and "a comforter is far from me" (1:16). The word menachem is built on the verb that opens Isaiah 40, "Comfort, comfort my people." Many readers hear that chapter as God's answer to this one, though that is a reading, not a quotation. In Jewish custom the seven Sabbaths after the Ninth of Av take their prophetic readings from Isaiah 40 on, which are called the Haftarot of Consolation.

p: Prophets call Judah's foreign allies her "lovers"; they were no help in 587/586.
b: In prophetic language a nation that trusts other nations for protection is a woman with lovers (Jeremiah 4:30; Ezekiel 23:5-9). The "lovers" are Egypt and the small neighbor kings who joined Judah's last revolt against Babylon (compare Jeremiah 27:1-3 and 4:17 in this book). Their promised help failed. The same word returns at 1:19.

t: Exile because of, after, or out of?
p: The Hebrew word before "suffering" can mean after, because of, or away from.
b: Mē'oni umērov 'avodah begins with the little word min, "from". It can mean "after affliction" (looking back at what she went through), "because of affliction" (driven out by it), or "away from affliction" (escaping it, which would fit only if exile were a refuge, as Judah finds it is not). The Plain English Translation keeps the middle sense. Exile happened in waves: 597 BC, 586 BC and a third deportation reported in Jeremiah 52:30 (2 Kings 24:14; 25:11).

p: Deuteronomy's curses say that in exile there will be no resting place.
b: The Hebrew word manoach is the one used in Deuteronomy 28:65: among the nations "you will find no rest, and there will be no resting place for the sole of your foot." The poet is telling what the curses of the covenant said would happen. The same chapter of Deuteronomy supplies the picture of a siege where parents eat their children (Deuteronomy 28:53-57; compare Lamentations 2:20 and Lamentations 4:10).

p: The Hebrew means tight spots, mountain passes or distress; the Greek reads "oppressors".
b: Bein hammetsarim is "between the narrow places", the same word as "straits" in Psalm 118:5. It paints a pursued woman cornered in a gorge. The Greek (as Swete prints it) reads "between those who oppress", which is a different pointing of the same consonants. See the variant entry.

p: Three times a year Israel went up to Jerusalem for a festival; now the roads are empty.
b: Mo'ed is an "appointed" time, and the three pilgrim festivals (Passover, Weeks, Booths) brought crowds up to Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 16:16). The Plain English Translation uses "festival" every time (1:4, 15; 2:6, 7, 22) so the reader can hear the word return in 1:15 and 2:22, where the LORD himself "calls a festival" against the city. Psalm 42:4 remembers the processions to the house of God that this verse misses.

p: Hebrew betulot are young unmarried women; the Plain English Translation says "young women" and keeps "virgin" for the city's title.
b: Betulah is a young woman of marrying age. Whether the word itself always means a woman who has had no sexual partner is argued; in Deuteronomy 22:19 and Leviticus 21:14 the context makes it so. The Plain English Translation says "young women" for the plural here, in 1:18, 2:10, 2:21 and 5:11, and translates the personified title betulat bat Tsiyyon "the virgin, Daughter Zion" (as elsewhere in the prophets, 1:15; 2:13) because the title treats the city as an unmarried daughter whose honor was kept until now.

p: The "head" and "tail" are Deuteronomy's picture of who rules and who serves.
b: In the covenant curses the foreigner becomes the head and Israel the tail (Deuteronomy 28:44). The poet takes the phrase as already fulfilled. A pointed idiom: "head" here means first place, as in Isaiah 9:14.

a: The LORD has given her sorrow
t: Who caused it? The first verdict
p: The poet says plainly that the LORD brought the city's grief, and keeps saying it.
b: The verb hogah "has given grief" is used again at 1:12 and 3:32-33. The book never lets the reader blame only Babylon or only Judah's politicians. Earlier prophets, from Moses' song (Deuteronomy 32:19-25) to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 5:19; 16:10-13), had told Judah that exile would be the LORD's own act. The poet agrees, and then asks God to look at what this means (1:9, 11). For how churches and synagogues have used this verdict, see the book-level "Where Christians differ" card.

p: Hebrew has separate words for rebellion, sin and guilt; the Plain English Translation keeps them apart.
b: Pesha', "rebellion", is the sharpest: deliberate revolt against a ruler (1:5, 14, 22; 3:42). Chet / chata', "sin", is missing the mark (1:8; 3:39; 4:6, 13, 22; 5:7, 16). 'Avon, "guilt", is the weight of wrong that is carried (2:14; 4:6, 13, 22; 5:7). The first is the one the poet uses for Jerusalem's treason against God. The Plain English Translation never uses one English word for two of them.

p: "Daughter Zion" is the city pictured as a daughter, a wife, a widow and a mother.
b: Bat Tsiyyon is literally "the daughter of Zion", but in Hebrew the genitive often says what a person is: "Zion, the daughter". Isaiah calls her a hut in a vineyard (Isaiah 1:8) and Zephaniah and Zechariah tell her to rejoice (Zephaniah 3:14; Zechariah 2:10). Lamentations uses the title again and again. The poems also say "Daughter Judah" (1:15; 2:2, 5), "Daughter Jerusalem" (2:13, 15), "Daughter Edom" (4:21-22) and "Daughter of my people", which the Plain English Translation renders "my dear people" (2:11). Dobbs-Allsopp has argued that the figure resembles the weeping city-goddess of Mesopotamian city laments, now made human; not every scholar accepts the link.
r: Isaiah 1:8; Isaiah 37:22; Micah 4:8; Zephaniah 3:14; Zechariah 2:10; Psalm 9:14

p: Niddah is the word for the uncleanness of a woman during her period; here it names Jerusalem herself.
b: Niddah belongs to the purity laws (Leviticus 15:19-30; 18:19), where it names the ritual uncleanness that kept a woman from the sanctuary for a time. Prophets use it for Israel's guilt (Ezekiel 36:17). In 1:8 the city has become a niddah, an "unclean thing", and in 1:17 she is the same among her neighbors. The poet says it was her sin that did it (1:8).

p: The stripped woman is a picture, but the poem also describes real events.
b: To strip a city was an ancient picture of conquest (Isaiah 47:3; Ezekiel 16:37-39; Hosea 2:10; Nahum 3:5). Reading 1:8-10, scholars warn against taking the verses only as metaphor. The poet moves without a break from the woman exposed to the sanctuary entered, the treasures taken and nations crossing a line the Law forbade. Soldiers did sack the temple (2 Kings 25:13-17), and the women of Judah were raped (5:11). Where the poem describes a woman violated, it is also describing what happened to women.

a: she never thought of how it would end
p: The same charge is made against Babylon in Isaiah 47:7 and against Israel in Deuteronomy 32:29.
b: Lo zakhrah 'acharitah says that she took no thought of what lay ahead. Moses' song wishes that Israel would understand and think about its end (Deuteronomy 32:29), and Isaiah says the same of Babylon (Isaiah 47:7). The charge is neither guilty-by-ignorance nor a theological trap: it describes a nation that thought the city could not fall (see 4:12).

p: The narrator's account breaks off and the city speaks to God for the first time.
b: Up to here the poet speaks about Zion in the third person. In the last line of 1:9 and in 1:11 the speaker says "my affliction" and "I", and addresses the LORD. The Hebrew gives no marker. Some commentators suppose a second voice (Zion) breaking in; Berlin and others see one poet moving between voices. The prayer "See, LORD" returns at 1:11, 1:20, 2:20 and 5:1. The Plain English Translation adds no quotation marks, so the reader hears the change as the Hebrew gives it.

p: Foreigners entered the temple, which the Law kept them out of.
b: Deuteronomy 23:3-4 bars Ammonites and Moabites "from the assembly of the LORD" to the tenth generation. The Babylonians did not only enter; they carried out the bronze and silver vessels and burned the house (2 Kings 25:9, 13-17; Jeremiah 52:17-23). Psalm 79:1 laments the same thing: the nations have entered God's inheritance and defiled his holy temple. The poet does not say that the sack was a surprise: it is an offense to a law he knew, which now seems to bind only the LORD's own people.

p: The Hebrew word can mean worthless or greedy; the city has been reduced to selling her treasures for bread.
b: Zolelah comes from a root meaning "be light, worthless" and is also used for a glutton (Deuteronomy 21:20). Jeremiah 15:19 sets "what is precious" against "what is worthless" (zol). The nearest sense here is worthless: the city whose treasures were once prized is now the one that gives them away for food (1:11).

p: The first Hebrew word is a puzzle; the Greek and Latin leave out "not".
b: The Hebrew lo 'alekhem is literally "not to you". It may be a question ("Is it nothing to you?", which is how the old hymns and sermons know it), a cry ("Let it not come upon you!"), or an ordinary statement with a missing verb. The Greek (as Swete prints Codex Vaticanus) and Jerome's Latin have no negative: "O all you who pass by on the road". The Qumran scroll 4Q111 has the Hebrew word lo here (in the transcription of 3Q3 the word is restored, not visible). Christian worship has long put these words in the mouth of Christ on the cross (the Latin "O vos omnes" in Holy Week); Jewish worship hears the city speaking after the Temple fell. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew with the negative as a question.

a: the day of his burning anger
p: This phrase returns at 1:12, 2:1, 2:21 and 2:22; the Plain English Translation uses "anger" only for one Hebrew word.
b: Yom charon 'appo, "day of his burning anger", comes from the prophets' "day of the LORD" (Zephaniah 2:2-3; Isaiah 13:13). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew words for God's anger apart: 'af "anger", charon 'af "burning anger", chemah "rage" (2:4; 4:11), 'evrah "fury" (2:2), and za'am "indignation" (2:6). See also the note at 2:2.

p: The Hebrew verb is unclear; the Greek has "brought it down".
b: Vayyirddenah is from radah, "rule, tread", so "and it overpowered them" (my bones). Another way to read the letters is from yarad, "come down", which the Greek follows ("he brought it down"). The picture of fire in the bones recalls Jeremiah's own fire shut up in his bones (Jeremiah 20:9). See the variant entry.

p: Judah's sins are tied together into a yoke the LORD lays on her neck.
b: A yoke was the wooden frame laid on an ox's neck, and it is a standard sign of slavery and submission. Deuteronomy's curses speak of an iron yoke (Deuteronomy 28:48); Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke to show Judah to submit to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:2, 12). Here the yoke is made from her own rebellions, which the LORD has woven with his own hand. In 3:27 the man carries a yoke "while he is young".

p: The book uses two names for God, and the Plain English Translation keeps them apart: "the LORD" (YHWH) and "the Lord" (Adonay).
b: YHWH is God's personal name, written "the LORD"; Adonay means "my lord" and is written "the Lord". In the whole book Adonay occurs 14 times: 1:14, 15 (twice); 2:1, 2, 5, 7, 18, 19, 20; 3:31, 36, 37, 58. Chapter 2 mixes the two from verse to verse: the Lord in 2:1, 2, 5, 7 and the LORD in 2:6, 8, 9, 17. The Plain English Translation does not smooth the shift. The scroll 4Q111 reads the divine name YHWH where the Masoretic Text has Adonay at 1:14; at 1:18 the transcription restores Adonay, and a restored word is not counted as the scroll's reading.

p: God treads Judah like grapes; the juice is blood.
b: Treading grapes became a picture of divine judgment: the Warrior who stained his clothes in Edom (Isaiah 63:1-6), the harvest of nations (Joel 3:13), and the great winepress of God's anger in Revelation (Revelation 14:19-20; 19:15). Here the press is trodden on the "virgin, Daughter Judah".

p: The doubled "eye" is in the Hebrew; the Greek has one.
b: The Hebrew says 'eini 'eini. The Greek, as Swete prints it, has one "eye", and some think the doubling is a copyist's slip; others take it as the poet's emphasis, a sob. Compare Jeremiah, who wished his head were water and his eye a spring of tears (Jeremiah 9:1; 8:18-9:3). See the variant entry.

p: The gesture is prayer or pleading for help.
b: Spreading the palms was a way of praying or asking for help (Exodus 9:29; Isaiah 1:15; Psalm 143:6). Here no one answers: the same sentence ends in the refrain "there is no one to comfort her".

p: The poem confesses that God is in the right, and goes on to ask that the nations be punished.
b: Tsaddiq hu YHWH is a confession of the kind made at the end of other disasters (Exodus 9:27; Ezra 9:15; Nehemiah 9:33; Daniel 9:14). The city says that God was in the right to punish her and, in the same breath, calls on the nations to look at her pain. The Talmud tells that the dying King Josiah, shot by Pharaoh's archers, said these words (Bavli Ta'anit 22b, which cites Lamentations 1:18). 4Q111 differs from the Masoretic Text at 1:17-18: in 1:17 it has a plus that includes the words "you are righteous, LORD", addressed to God, and in 1:18 it has "righteous is he" with the next word restored. The scroll is damaged, and the plus may be an intrusion of the confession of 1:18 or may reflect a different arrangement of the verses, so the Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text. See the variant entry at 1:17.

p: Hebrew marah means to defy or be stubborn; it is not the same word as rebellion.
b: Marah is the verb of the stubborn son (Deuteronomy 21:18-20) and of Moses and Aaron at Meribah (Numbers 20:24). The phrase pihu is literally "his mouth", meaning what he said. The Plain English Translation keeps marah ("defy", 1:18, 20; 3:42) apart from pesha' ("rebellion"). The poem confesses defiance, the sin of a servant who has heard and not obeyed.

a: Outside, the sword takes away children
p: The line repeats Moses' song, where the sword bereaves outside and terror waits indoors.
b: Deuteronomy 32:25 says that outside the sword will bereave and in the inner rooms there will be terror. The poet has taken a threat and found it fulfilled. The Hebrew verb shikkelah means to make childless; the Plain English Translation says "takes away children" without adding "mothers", which the Hebrew does not say.

a: now let them be like me
p: The city asks God to do to her enemies what he did to her.
b: The prayer that follows (1:21-22) and the longer one at 3:64-66 are of the kind found in the curse psalms: Psalm 137:8-9, Psalm 79:6, 12, Jeremiah 18:21-23. The poet does not ask for her own revenge; she asks God to act, since the nations "are glad that you did it". The text has no sense that God owes her anything more than justice. How churches and synagogues have prayed or not prayed such words is on the topic page; see the card at 3:64.

p: Chapter 2 gives each verse the next Hebrew letter; here pe comes before ayin.
b: Chapter 2 is a second alphabet poem, with one letter to each verse, alef at 2:1 to tav at 2:22. Here pe comes before ayin (2:16 pe, 2:17 ayin), the reverse of chapter 1, and so in chapters 3 and 4. English cannot copy the letters, so the Plain English Translation does not try; the chapter page lists all 22 Hebrew first words. The same form appears in Psalm 119, Proverbs 31:10-31 and Nahum 1:2-8. Like chapter 1 and unlike chapter 4, each verse has three lines in this Plain English Translation.

p: The verb is unique in the Bible; it seems to come from the word for cloud.
b: The verb ya'ib occurs only here. The best guess is that it is built on 'av, "cloud", so "he clouded over"; the Greek (as Swete prints it) has "darkened". The cloud once showed God's presence at Sinai and in the temple (Exodus 19:9; 1 Kings 8:10-12). Now it is a cloud of anger over the city; in 3:44 the man says God has wrapped himself in a cloud so that prayer cannot get through.

p: The "footstool" is the ark or the temple or Zion; God did not think of it on the day of anger.
b: Hadom raglav, "the footstool of his feet", is the place where God's feet rest on earth. It names the ark (1 Chronicles 28:2), the sanctuary (Psalm 132:7) or Zion (Psalm 99:5, with the call to worship at his footstool); Isaiah 66:1 asks what house could hold the one whose footstool is the earth. The pain of the verse is that God has hurled the beauty of Israel down and has not thought of his own footstool.

p: The phrase may mean the temple, Jerusalem, the ark or the king.
b: Tif'eret Yisra'el is a title the Hebrew Bible does not explain. It has been taken as the temple (Isaiah 64:11, the holy and beautiful house), as the ark (Psalm 78:61, where God gives his glory into captivity), as the city, or as David's line (compare 2 Samuel 1:19). "From heaven to earth" points to something that stood high.

p: Each Hebrew word for anger gets one English word in the Plain English Translation.
b: The Hebrew has many words for God's anger. The Plain English Translation gives each one English word: 'af "anger" (2:1, 6, 21, 22; 3:43, 66), charon 'af "burning anger" (1:12; 2:3; 4:11), chemah "rage" (2:4; 4:11), 'evrah "fury" (2:2; 3:1), za'am "indignation" (2:6), Chapter 2 piles them up.

p: "Swallow up" (bala') is a key verb in chapter 2.
b: Bala', "swallow", is used for the LORD in 2:2, 5, 8 and for the enemy in 2:16, and again in Jeremiah's picture of Nebuchadnezzar swallowing Jerusalem like a monster (Jeremiah 51:34). The poem has the LORD, not the enemy, as the one swallowing, until the enemies echo him: "We have swallowed her!" (2:16).

a: treated the kingdom and its princes as unholy
p: To profane is to make ordinary what was set apart.
b: Chillel is the verb for making holy things common (Leviticus 19:12; 21:12). God treats his own anointed kingdom as common ground.

p: A horn is a sign of strength, like the horns of an ox.
b: A raised horn is strength and victory (1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 75:10); a cut-off horn is defeat (Jeremiah 48:25). At 2:17 the enemy's horn is lifted.

p: God's right hand once saved Israel; now he holds it back.
b: God's right hand was the hand of the exodus (Exodus 15:6). Psalm 74:11 asks why God holds back his hand, his right hand. Here the poet says the LORD did just that when the enemy came on.

p: The poem says that the LORD acted like a warrior against his own people, and says it again in 2:5.
b: The LORD as a warrior who fights for Israel is well known (Exodus 15:3). Here the picture is reversed: he strings his bow and takes his stand "like an enemy" (2:4, 5). Earlier prophets had threatened it: the LORD says he himself will fight against Jerusalem (Jeremiah 21:5), and Isaiah says the LORD turned and became Israel's enemy (Isaiah 63:10). Job says God treats him as his enemy (Job 13:24). The poem does not explain the reversal. It describes it, and in 3:1-18 a single man says it of himself.

p: The same phrase is used of Ezekiel's wife, who died the day the siege began.
b: Machmadde 'ayin is "what the eye delights in". In Ezekiel 24:16-18 the LORD takes Ezekiel's wife, "the delight of your eyes", on the day the siege of Jerusalem begins, and forbids him to mourn. The poet says the same loss has now come to the whole city.

p: The Hebrew has two nearly identical words, like "mourning and moaning".
b: Ta'aniyyah va'aniyyah is a rhyming pair from the root of "sigh". Isaiah uses it for Ariel, the city of David (Isaiah 29:2). The Plain English Translation tries to keep the echo.

p: God's "booth" is the temple; the Hebrew for the comparison is uncertain, and the Greek reads "vine".
b: Sukkah (booth) is a hut of branches, like the shelter in a vineyard (Isaiah 1:8) or the booths of the festival of Booths. The poet calls God's house his booth, and then says he has torn it down. The Hebrew kaggan can be "like a garden", but many think the word has changed: the Greek has "like a vine". The Plain English Translation says "garden hut" to carry the sense of a flimsy shelter. The verb vayyachmos comes from chamas, "violence". The word translated "the place where he meets his people" is mo'ed, the same as "festival"; the Greek takes it that way. See the variant entry. The terms miqdash "sanctuary", mishkan "dwelling" and sukkah "booth" are used separately in this book.

p: The two things Israel kept, the festivals and the Sabbath, are now forgotten.
b: Hosea had spoken of the LORD ending all of Israel's celebration, "her festivals, her new moons, her sabbaths" (Hosea 2:11). The poem says that forgetting has happened, and that the LORD has made it happen: he has taken away the occasions of worship before he took the city.

a: Voices rang out in the LORD's house
p: The enemy's war cry in the temple is like the noise of a festival crowd.
b: Psalm 74:4 says that God's foes roared in the middle of his meeting place and set up their own signs there. The poet turns the sound of a festival into the sound of the enemy.

p: A line used to build is here used to tear down.
b: A measuring line marks the size of something to build or to destroy. The LORD stretches one over Samaria and Jerusalem in 2 Kings 21:13; Isaiah 34:11 uses the line of confusion; Amos 7:7-9 has the plumb line.

p: "Torah" here is the priests' teaching, not a book; it ends along with prophecy.
b: Torah here means priestly teaching and answers given on God's behalf, as in the prophets' complaint that "law will perish from the priest, vision from the prophet" (Ezekiel 7:26; Jeremiah 18:18). The Plain English Translation says "instruction" and not "law", as it does in Isaiah. The poet is not saying that the Law of Moses was lost, but that no one can now tell the people what God says.

p: Dust, sackcloth and sitting on the ground are signs of grief.
b: Mourners sat on the ground, threw dust on their heads and wore coarse sackcloth (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12-13; Ezekiel 27:30-31). The elders, who would normally sit at the gate to judge, now sit in silence.

a: my liver is poured out on the ground
p: The Hebrew ties feeling to the body: eyes, bowels, liver.
b: Kaved is the liver, the heavy organ. To pour it out on the ground is to be emptied of everything. Job says God pours out his gall on the ground (Job 16:13). The Plain English Translation keeps "liver" instead of "bile" or "heart".

a: the ruin of my dear people
p: Hebrew says "the daughter of my people"; the Plain English Translation says "my dear people" and uses "ruin" for shever.
b: Bat 'ammi is literally "the daughter of my people", with the same pattern as "Daughter Zion": the people are the daughter. Jeremiah uses it often (Jeremiah 8:11, 19, 21; 9:1) and the Plain English Translation renders it the same way. Shever means a break or fracture: "ruin" (2:11, 13; 3:47, 48; 4:10), the same Hebrew word as the "breaking" of Jeremiah 8:21, the "broken place" that the prophets bandage as a trifle in Jeremiah 6:14, and the "ruin" of Lamentations 2:13. Here the speaker is the poet, not a character in the poem.

p: Jeremiah asked the same question about the same wound.
b: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" Jeremiah asked (Jeremiah 8:22). Here no healer is named. In Jeremiah 30:12-17 the LORD says the wound is incurable and then promises to heal it. The poem stops at the question.

a: Your ruin is as big as the sea
p: The Greek reads "a cup" for "sea".
b: The Hebrew kayyam is "like the sea". The Greek, as printed by Swete, reads "the cup of your ruin has grown great", which suggests a Hebrew word for "cup" (kos); the Latin and Masoretic Text keep "sea". Both pictures fit: the cup of wrath (4:21), or a wound as wide as an ocean. See the variant entry.

p: The prophets told Jerusalem pleasant things; the Hebrew calls them empty and plastered over.
b: Shav vatafel: "emptiness and whitewash". Tafel is the plaster Ezekiel says false prophets put on a weak wall (Ezekiel 13:10-15). Jeremiah says the same: prophets who said "Peace" when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 23:16-17; 29:8-9). The same charge returns in 4:13.

p: The idiom may mean "restore your fortunes"; it is spelled two ways in the manuscripts.
b: Lehashiv shevutekh is the stock phrase "to turn the captivity" (Deuteronomy 30:3; Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3). It may mean to bring back the exiles or to turn fortunes around. The Leningrad Codex and other copies spell the word two ways (shevut and shevit), which makes no difference in the sense. The prophets' failure was not that they said too little about judgment but that they did not name the guilt that needed to be dealt with.

p: "Madduchim" may mean "misleading" or "leading to exile".
b: Maddu'chim comes from nadach, "drive away". It can mean oracles that lead people astray or oracles whose results were driving the people into exile. The Greek (as Swete prints it) has "expulsions", which takes it the second way; the Plain English Translation follows the first.

p: The gesture of mockery here is the one used at the cross.
b: The same gestures of scorn appear in Psalm 22:7, Jeremiah 18:16 and 19:8, and Zephaniah 2:15. In the passion accounts passers-by "shake their heads" at Jesus (Matthew 27:39; Mark 15:29). That is an echo, not a quotation: the Gospel writers do not name Lamentations.

t: Perfect in beauty, joy of all the earth
p: These are the titles the psalms gave Zion.
b: Psalm 50:2 calls Zion "perfect in beauty" and Psalm 48:2 calls it "the joy of all the earth". The mockers quote the praise back at the ruin. Ezekiel uses the same words for Tyre (Ezekiel 27:3), another city whose pride fell.

p: What the LORD did to the city is what he said, long before, that he would do.
b: "Which he commanded in the days of old" points to the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:14-39; Deuteronomy 28:15-68) and to prophets from Moses to Jeremiah. Zechariah 1:6 asks whether the prophets' words did not overtake the fathers. The poem does not blame the enemy here, only says that the LORD did what he said.

a: Their hearts cry out to the Lord
p: The verse has no clear subject; it shifts at once to speak to the city's wall.
b: The Hebrew says "their heart cried out to the Lord". Who is "their"? It may be the survivors; it may be the people in 2:17; and the next words address the wall of Zion. Commentators (Hillers, Berlin, Salters) differ on whether the text has been changed or whether the poem simply shifts from description to command. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and does not guess.

a: Lift up your hands to him
p: Lifting the hands to God was a posture of prayer; 3:41 uses it again.
b: Lifted hands appear in prayer in Psalm 28:2, Psalm 63:4 and Psalm 134:2. Here the prayer is not for the city but for the children. The "night watches" are the three or four periods into which the night was divided; the call is to begin the prayer at the start of the first watch and keep it up (compare Psalm 119:148).

a: Should women eat their own offspring
p: The Torah said it would happen in a siege; 2 Kings tells of one such case; Lamentations says it happened.
b: Moses had named this horror as a curse (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57). Second Kings 6:28-29 tells of two women in a famine in Samaria, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel repeat the threat (Jeremiah 19:9; Ezekiel 5:10). Lamentations 4:10 says it happened. Readers have taken it as plain history, as the fulfillment of the curse and a way of describing the worst that can happen, or as exaggeration; the Hebrew gives no hint that it is figure. Josephus tells of a similar case in the Roman siege of 70 AD (War 6.3.4), which readers have often set beside it. The question "Should women eat...?" is a protest, asked of God.

p: The Hebrew word is rare and may mean children carried in the hands.
b: Tippuchim may come from tephach, "handbreadth", for a child small enough to be held in the palm, or from a verb "to carry" (the Greek has "children they have nursed"). The sense is a young child, wholly dependent on the mother.

t: Priest and prophet killed in the sanctuary
p: The Babylonians killed the temple priests, and the poet protests that the sanctuary was a place of sacred refuge.
b: Second Kings 25:18-21 tells how the chief priest Seraiah and other leaders were taken to Riblah and put to death; Second Chronicles 36:17 says the Babylonian king killed young men "in the house of their sanctuary". For the Israelite the sanctuary was a place of safety; the killing there is part of the offense.

p: "Magor missaviv" was Jeremiah's catchphrase; here the LORD calls terrors as if inviting guests.
b: Magor missaviv, "Terror All Around", is a phrase of Jeremiah's (Jeremiah 6:25; 20:3, 10; 46:5; 49:29; Psalm 31:13), which his enemies threw back at him. Here the poet makes it plural, "my terrors", and has the LORD summon them "as for a festival day". The festival (mo'ed) that had gathered pilgrims now gathers terrors.

p: Chapter 3 begins with a man who says "I"; readers have named at least six people he could be.
b: Haggever, "the man", is a strong or able man (not 'adam, a human being, or 'ish, a husband or man; it returns in 3:27 and 3:35, 39). Views: Jeremiah, on the old tradition of authorship; a king, such as Jehoiachin or Zedekiah (compare 4:20); a survivor, a man who saw the siege; a soldier, the male counterpart of Daughter Zion (some modern readers take the Hebrew word as "strong man" or "warrior"); the nation speaking as one man, which fits the way the "I" turns into "we" at 3:40; and the suffering righteous, a Job-like figure whose complaint (3:1-18) is close to Job 16 and 19. Westermann read the chapter as an individual's psalm of lament. Christian readers have heard Christ in it (see 3:30). The text names no one, and the Plain English Translation does not add a name.

p: Chapter 3 is an alphabet poem with three verses for each of the 22 letters.
b: Verses 1-3 each begin with alef, verses 4-6 with bet, and so on to tav at 64-66. The Plain English Translation gives each triplet a heading with the letter and a short title, the way it does for Psalm 119, and the chapter page lists all 22. Because all three lines of a stanza begin with the same letter in Hebrew, the chapter is tighter than 1, 2 and 4. In 2, 3 and 4 the letter pe comes before ayin (3:46-48 pe; 3:49-51 ayin), while in chapter 1 ayin comes first; the topic page on alphabet poems records this order. Commentators disagree on why: a second alphabet order that was also in use (put forward by some scholars), a scribe's switch, or a deliberate break. No view is settled.

p: A rod is a stick for striking; Isaiah calls Assyria God's rod.
b: Shevet is the shepherd's or ruler's stick, used for discipline (Proverbs 22:15). Isaiah 10:5 calls Assyria "the rod of my anger", a foreign army used as God's instrument. "Fury" is 'evrah, as in 2:2.

a: walk in darkness, with no light
p: Job says the same of God.
b: Compare Job 19:8, where God "has set darkness on my paths", and Job 30:26. Amos had called the day of the LORD "darkness, not light" (Amos 5:18-20). The man's life is that day.

p: The Hebrew rosh is a bitter plant or its poison.
b: Rosh is a bitter, poisonous plant, often paired with wormwood (Deuteronomy 29:18; Jeremiah 9:15). At 3:19 the pair comes back: "wormwood and poison". The Plain English Translation uses "poison" every time.

p: The same words are in Psalm 143:3, and can also mean "dead forever".
b: Kemetei 'olam may be "like the dead of long ago" (the long-buried) or "like those dead forever". Psalm 143:3 has the same phrase. The Greek, as printed by Swete, reads "like the dead of the age".

p: Zedekiah and Samson were both bound in bronze.
b: Bronze fetters bound Samson (Judges 16:21) and King Zedekiah when Nebuchadnezzar blinded him and took him to Babylon (2 Kings 25:7). The man's chain is a king's chain; this is one reason some readers think of Zedekiah.

p: The man says God shuts out his prayer; 3:55-57 says God heard.
b: The same book that says the LORD "shuts out" prayer (3:8) and wraps himself in cloud so no prayer passes through (3:44) also says "You heard my voice" and "You drew near" (3:56-57). The man does not resolve the two. Lament allows both to be said in one breath: that God is not answering, and that God has answered before.

p: God as a hunting animal appears in Hosea and Job.
b: Hosea 13:7-8 has the LORD as a lion, leopard and bear, and Job 10:16 says God hunts him like a lion. The Leningrad Codex spells "lion" differently from the Qere ('aryeh and 'ari); the sense is the same.

p: Job says God's archers surround him and pierce his kidneys.
b: The Hebrew says he drove "the sons of his quiver" into the kidneys, a way of saying arrows. The kidneys were the seat of the inner life. Job 16:12-13 has the same picture, and Psalm 38:2 has God's arrows sinking in. In Deuteronomy 32:23 God spends his arrows on Israel.

p: Jeremiah said the same about himself.
b: Compare Jeremiah 20:7, where Jeremiah says he is a laughingstock all day. If the man is not Jeremiah, he suffers as Jeremiah did. The word "mocking song" returns at 3:63.

p: A bitter plant; in the Bible it is the taste of judgment.
b: La'anah is the bitter plant wormwood. Deuteronomy 29:18 warns of a root that bears poison and wormwood; Jeremiah says the LORD will feed the prophets wormwood (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15). Revelation 8:11 names a star Wormwood.

p: To eat gravel is a picture of the worst food there is.
b: The word chatsats is gravel. Proverbs 20:17 says that the bread of deceit tastes sweet and then the mouth is filled with gravel. The Greek, as Swete prints it, has "pebble".

p: The Hebrew netsach can mean endurance, splendor or forever.
b: Netsach is used for "lasting", "victory" or "forever" in different places. In 1 Samuel 15:29 it is a title for God. The Plain English Translation reads "my strength to endure", but "my splendor" and "my lasting" are also given. What is gone, he says, is both his endurance and his hope from the LORD.

a: This I bring back to my heart
p: The verse that turns the chapter uses the same idiom as Deuteronomy 4:39.
b: Zot 'ashiv 'el libbi is "this I bring back to my heart", the idiom of taking something to heart, as in Deuteronomy 4:39 and Deuteronomy 30:1. Many English Bibles say "call to mind". What he recalls is not new information; it is what he has said in 3:19-20 plus the next verses. The man does not argue himself out of grief. He chooses what to remember.

p: Two Hebrew words are translated wait, and a third means in silence.
b: Yachal (3:21, 24, 26) and qavah (3:25, "wait with hope", literally stretched toward) are both "wait" in the Plain English Translation; dumam is "in silence" (3:26); darash, "look for", is separate (3:25). They are the words of the psalms of waiting (Psalm 130:5-7; Psalm 37:7).

t: The LORD's acts of loyal love
p: The Hebrew is plural: the many deeds in which loyal love shows itself.
b: Chasdei YHWH is plural: not a feeling but acts. It comes from the creed of Exodus 34:6-7 ("abounding in loyal love"), which the prophets and psalms quote (Joel 2:13; Psalm 103:8). "The acts of the LORD's loyal love" is a phrase of praise (Psalm 89:1; Isaiah 63:7). The Hebrew has "we are not finished" (first person plural); the Greek manuscripts that supply this verse (Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus), the Peshitta, the Targum and some Hebrew manuscripts are reported to read "they are not finished", with the acts of loyal love as the subject. See the variant entry.

a: his compassions have not run out
p: Rachamim comes from the word for the womb: a mother's feeling for her child.
b: Rachamim is related to rechem, "womb", and means the tenderness of a parent (Psalm 103:13). It comes from the creed's "compassionate" (rachum, Exodus 34:6). In 4:10 the same root names the "compassionate" women who boiled their children, which the poem sets without comment beside this verse.

p: The hymn takes its line from here; in the Hebrew the faithfulness is God's, and the speaker switches to "you".
b: 'Emunah is firmness, reliability. The sentence switches from "he" to "you" in mid-verse, the voice of a person who has stopped talking about God and begun to talk to him. The hymn "Great Is Thy Faithfulness" (words by Thomas Chisholm, 1923) takes its title from this line. The "new every morning" is literally "new for the mornings", plural, each morning.

p: The Levites had no land; the LORD was their share.
b: The priests and Levites received no tribal land, because the LORD himself was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9). The psalmists claim the same: Psalm 16:5, Psalm 73:26, Psalm 119:57, Psalm 142:5. A man who has lost everything says that God is what he has left.

p: To seek God is a basic phrase of devotion in the Bible.
b: The Hebrew has the verb darash, "seek". Seeking the LORD is the answer promised to those in exile (Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13). The Ketiv spells a singular, "the one who waits for him", and the Qere "those who wait for him"; the sense is the same.

p: Silence before God is a psalm theme.
b: Psalm 62:1 speaks of a soul that waits in silence for God alone (the Hebrew word dumiyyah has the same root as dumam). "The LORD's rescue" is yeshu'ah, as in Exodus 14:13 where Moses tells Israel to stand still and see the LORD's rescue.

p: The yoke is discipline, patiently borne.
b: A young ox is yoked to learn the work. Verses 27-30 give four pictures of patient endurance: the yoke, silence, the mouth in the dust, the cheek turned. They read differently in different traditions, from a call to accept punishment, to a school of wisdom, to preparation for resistance. The same book also says the yoke is the LORD's doing (1:14).

p: The prophets also say "perhaps" about God's mercy.
b: 'Ulay, "perhaps", is the prophets' word for mercy not yet promised: Amos 5:15, Joel 2:14 ("Who knows? He may turn") and Zephaniah 2:3. Putting the mouth in the dust is the gesture of the beaten (Micah 7:17). Codex Vaticanus, as Swete prints it, has no text at 3:29 (as at 3:22-24), so the Greek of this verse is not used here; no difference of sense is claimed for it.

a: hand his cheek to whoever hits him
p: Isaiah 50:6 and Matthew 5:39 turn up beside this verse.
b: Isaiah's servant gives his cheeks to those who pluck out his beard (Isaiah 50:6); Job complains that they strike his cheek in scorn (Job 16:10). Jesus says to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39; Luke 6:29), and Christian readers hear in the suffering man a picture of Christ's passion (Matthew 27:30; John 18:22). That is a reading laid over the verse, not something it says. Some Jewish readers (and some Christians) hear in it a call to bear shame without revenge, and others hear only the man's despair.

p: The turn: God's anger has a limit.
b: "The Lord does not reject forever" is close to Psalm 77:7-9 and Psalm 94:14 and to Isaiah 54:7-8, where God says he left Zion only for a brief moment. In 5:20 the people will ask the opposite: "Why do you forget us forever?" The book holds both.

a: it is not from his heart that he afflicts
p: God does afflict, but not as something he enjoys; the verse is one of the book's hardest.
b: Millibbo is literally "from his heart". It can mean "willingly", "for the pleasure of it", or "as his own first wish". Isaiah 28:21 calls God's judgment his "strange work", and Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11 say he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; Hosea 11:8 has his heart turn within him. The Hebrew verb 'anah is "afflict" (it is the same letters as "answer", and the Greek of Codex Vaticanus, as Swete prints it, reads "answered from his heart"). The Ketiv of 3:32 has "his loyal love" (chasdo) and the Qere "his acts of loyal love" (chasadav); the Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as in 3:22. This verse is the heart of the book-level question of how God can send suffering; see the card at 3:37.

a: does the Lord not see it
t: Three wrongs: does the Lord not see?
p: The three infinitives are wrongs the Lord does not approve of, or the Hebrew is a question; the Hebrew has no question mark.
b: Verses 34-36 name three wrongs: trampling prisoners, bending a person's rights, and subverting a lawsuit. The last words are Adonay lo ra'ah, "the Lord has not seen". Views: a rhetorical question ("does the Lord not see?", the Plain English Translation); a statement that the Lord does not look on such things with approval; or a statement that God cannot be accused of causing them. Who does these wrongs? Many take it as the enemy, and some as God himself in 3:1-18; the next two verses (3:37-38) are a reply either way.

a: Who ever spoke, and it happened
t: Does God cause good and evil?
p: Verses 37-38 say that nothing happens unless the Lord commands it, and that both good and troubles come from the Most High.
b: Mi zeh amar vattehi Adonay lo tsivvah: "Who has spoken and it came to be, unless the Lord ordered it?" The answer assumed is no one. And 3:38 asks whether it is not from the Most High's mouth that both "the troubles" (ra'ot) and "the good" come. The sentence has been read as a statement of complete divine control, as a protest, as the poet repeating the people's own creed before he turns on it, and as a challenge to the idea that God rules every outcome (3:34-36 shows wrongs he does not approve). Isaiah 45:7 and Amos 3:6 say similar things. Christian churches answer very differently what this means for God and evil; see the card below.
orig: מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת וְהַטּוֹב

t: Why should a living person grumble?
p: The verb is the one used for the grumbling of Israel in the wilderness.
b: Yit'onen is "grumble" (Numbers 11:1). Read with 3:42 ("we have rebelled") it is a call to look at oneself. The Hebrew has "his sin" (Ketiv) or "his sins" (Qere). "Sin" (chet') can also mean the penalty of sin, as in Zechariah 14:19, so the clause may mean: why should a living person complain about his punishment?

p: From here the speaker says "we", and the call is to examine and return.
b: The speaker changes from "I" to "we" (3:40-47): the man now speaks for the community, or the community takes the microphone from him. "Search" (chaphas) is what Haggai tells the returned exiles to do with their ways (Haggai 1:5). "Return" (shuv) is Jeremiah's word (Jeremiah 3:12-14); in 5:21 the community will ask God to do the returning for them.

p: Right after the confession the people say God has not forgiven; the word "you" is stressed in Hebrew.
b: The verb salach "forgive" has only God as its subject. Solomon prayed that God would forgive exiles who repented (1 Kings 8:46-50), and 2 Kings 24:4 says the LORD would not forgive the blood Manasseh shed. The poem reaches the same point: they have confessed, and he has not. It may be an accusation, a statement of fact, or the groundwork for the prayer at 5:21-22. The doubled "we" and "you" shows the contrast the Hebrew draws.

p: Two near-synonyms: shet (devastation) and shever (ruin).
b: Shet ("devastation") and shever ("ruin", the book's word for a people's broken state, as at 2:11, 13 and 3:48) are close in meaning and often merged in English. The Plain English Translation keeps them apart: shever is "ruin" every time in this book, and shet is "devastation".

a: Streams of water run down my eye
p: The weeping poet recalls the weeping prophet.
b: Jeremiah wished that his eyes were a fountain of tears for the slain of his people (Jeremiah 9:1; 13:17; 14:17). Psalm 119:136 says streams of water run down the psalmist's eyes. The likeness helped lead tradition to Jeremiah as the author.

p: Pit, stone and water are the pictures here; Psalms and Jonah use the same ones.
b: Birds were caught in snares (Psalm 124:7; Proverbs 6:5). The pit, the stone and the flood (3:53-54) match Psalm 69:2, 14-15 (where "without cause" also appears, Psalm 69:4) and Jonah 2:3-6. The scroll 3Q3 preserves 3:52-62 and, in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription, differs from the Masoretic Text only in spelling. The scene is a poet's picture, not necessarily a literal pit (compare Jeremiah 38:6, where Jeremiah was lowered into a cistern).

p: The man's words are the words of Psalm 88 and Isaiah 53:8.
b: Nigzarti, "I am cut off", is used of the servant in Isaiah 53:8 ("cut off from the land of the living") and in Psalm 88:5. It is a picture of death before one's time.

p: God's words in this verse may be a priest's answer in worship.
b: Verses 55-60 use verbs in the perfect tense: "you heard", "you drew near". They can mean that God answered in the past, or that the man is so sure of an answer that he speaks as if it had come. Begrich argued that in the temple a priest or prophet spoke a message of reassurance (the "salvation oracle") to a person who had prayed, and "do not fear" is its stock phrase (Isaiah 41:10, 14; 43:1). Whether that oracle is a real event here or a recollection is not clear from the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew verb is the family rescuer's, as Boaz for Ruth.
b: Ga'al is what a close relative did to buy back a person or property (Ruth 4:4; Leviticus 25:25). God is the one who "redeems" (Psalm 103:4; Job 19:25). The man is no longer facing God across a gap; he is under family protection.

p: The man ends with a prayer that God do to his enemies what they have done; the Hebrew verbs may be a wish or a promise.
b: The three verbs ("you will repay", "you will give", "you will chase") look like a statement of what God will do. They may be taken as wishes, as a prayer that God act. Deuteronomy 32:35 and 41-43 has God taking vengeance, and Psalm 137:8 and Psalm 79:6, 12 ask for it. In Romans 12:19 Paul tells believers to leave vengeance to God, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35. In the Hebrew, vengeance belongs to God, and the man does not do it himself. How the churches use such words differs; see the card.

p: The Hebrew word is rare; the Greek reads "toil of heart".
b: Meginnat lev occurs only here. It is related to magen, "shield", and may mean a covering or veil over the heart, a hardness, a darkness. The Greek, as Swete prints it, has "a shield, toil of heart". The meaning is that the enemies will be unable to see or feel what is happening to them.

a: How the gold has lost its shine
p: Chapter 4 begins with "How!" again and runs the alphabet at one letter for each verse.
b: 'Eikhah opens the verse (and again in 4:2). Each verse has two lines in this Plain English Translation, with the second shorter (chapters 1 and 2 have three), and the letters run alef to tav. In chapter 4, pe comes before ayin (4:16 and 4:17). Gold that has gone dull is a picture for a ruined people or for the temple's gold (1 Kings 6:20-22).

p: The "holy stones" may be the temple's stones or the jewels of the priest's breastplate.
b: 'Avne qodesh is open: the temple's building stones (the temple was burned and torn down, 2 Kings 25:9-10), the gems of the priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17-21), or the "sons of Zion" (4:2) as holy stones. Micah 3:12 had said Zion would be plowed as a field. They are "strewn" at the head (corner) of every street.

p: The word is rare; Job uses it to say wisdom cannot be paid for with gold.
b: Mesullaim "weighed" appears also in Job 28:16, 19. Zion's sons were worth their weight in gold; now they are "pottery jars", a cheap, easily broken thing (Isaiah 30:14; Jeremiah 19:11).

p: The Hebrew consonants spell "sea monsters"; the vowels turn it into "jackals".
b: The Leningrad Codex writes the animal as tanin (the written form, Ketiv, which looks like a singular of tanninim, "sea monsters" or "serpents") and reads it tannim, "jackals" (the form read aloud, Qere). The Plain English Translation follows the Qere because the verse is about animals that nurse their young; Greek ("dragons") and Latin ("lamias") took it as a monster or serpent. There is a second Ketiv/Qere in the verse: written ki ("for"), read ka- ("like"), in "like the ostriches" (ya'en); the Plain English Translation follows the Qere, and the sense is not changed. The ostrich is the bird that, in Job 39:13-18, leaves her eggs on the ground and treats her young hard. See the variant entry.

p: Nobles clutching a rubbish heap reverses the psalms' promise.
b: The LORD "lifts the needy from the ash heap" (1 Samuel 2:8; Psalm 113:7). In Lamentations the children raised in crimson clutch at the ash heaps. Crimson was a royal and wealthy dye.

a: greater than the sin of Sodom
p: The poem says Jerusalem's guilt is greater than Sodom's; Ezekiel says the same.
b: Sodom's end was sudden (Genesis 19:24-25). Jerusalem's was slow and agonized. Ezekiel 16:48-50 says that Sodom did not do what Jerusalem has done, and Jeremiah 23:14 calls Jerusalem's prophets like Sodom. Here "guilt" ('avon) is probably the punishment as well: the guilt and its penalty. The city that burned in a moment suffered less than the city that starved for months.

a: with no hand turned against it
p: The Hebrew may mean no hand attacked it, or no hands wrung in grief.
b: Velo-chalu vah yadayim: the verb comes from chul, "turn, writhe". It can mean that Sodom was destroyed with no human hand against it (God alone, in a moment), or that no one wrung their hands over it (the suffering was too brief). The Greek has "no one labored on it". The Plain English Translation keeps the first.

p: The Hebrew nezir is the word for a Nazirite, but can also mean a prince set apart.
b: Nazir is the Nazirite who took a vow (Numbers 6), but the word also means someone "set apart", as Joseph is called the nazir of his brothers (Genesis 49:26). The Greek and the Latin read "Nazirites", and the Plain English Translation reads "nobles", which fits the pictures of rank in 4:5. The Qumran scroll 5Q6 preserves 4:7, and in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription the word is restored, not visible.

p: The poem uses a word for compassion that it also uses for God.
b: The women are rachamaniyyot, from the same root as God's compassion in 3:22. Deuteronomy 28:56-57 speaks of the tender woman who will eat her child in the siege, and 2 Kings 6:28-29 tells of two women in the famine of Samaria. The poet does not say this happened to everyone; he says it happened. The Plain English Translation and the notes do not soften it. Readers have taken it as history, as covenant curse, or as the poem's worst image.

t: The city that could not fall
p: Many in Judah believed God would never let Jerusalem fall.
b: The songs of Zion said God was in the city and it would not be shaken (Psalm 46:5-7; Psalm 48:4-8; Psalm 76:1-3), and in 701 BC the Assyrian king did not take it (Isaiah 37:33-35). Jeremiah mocked those who chanted "the temple of the LORD" as a charm (Jeremiah 7:4). The poet says the kings of the earth shared the belief. The "royal Zion" tradition is the mood the book is writing against.

t: The sins of prophets and priests
p: The poem names the religious leaders as those who shed the blood of the righteous.
b: Views: the leaders did literally kill the righteous (the priests and prophets who tried Jeremiah and demanded his death, Jeremiah 26:7-11; Manasseh's innocent blood, 2 Kings 21:16); they led the people astray so the innocent died in the siege; or this is a stock charge (Ezekiel 22:26-28; Jeremiah 23:11). The charge against prophets repeats 2:14. A traditional Christian reading hears an echo in Jesus' words against those who killed the prophets (Matthew 23:34-35), though Lamentations is not cited there.

p: The cry is that of a person with a skin disease, or people shouting at the leaders.
b: A person with a skin disease had to cry "Unclean, unclean!" (Leviticus 13:45-46). Here the cry is thrown at the blood-stained, blind priests and prophets. Views: the people drive away the leaders; the leaders themselves cry out to keep others off; or others cry at the fleeing survivors in general. Isaiah 52:11 uses the same words in the other direction ("Go out, go out, touch nothing unclean"). The "nations" (4:15) say the exiles cannot stay.

a: a nation that does not save
p: The nation may be Egypt, whose army briefly drew the Babylonians away.
b: In 588 BC the Egyptian army marched out and the Babylonians lifted the siege for a time (Jeremiah 37:5-11), but Egypt did not save the city. Isaiah and Ezekiel called Egypt a broken reed (Isaiah 36:6; Ezekiel 29:6-7). Many take the "nation that could not save" to be Egypt; others think of any ally, since the poet names none.

a: The breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed
p: The poem mourns a captured king; scholars and traditions name different men.
b: Meshiach YHWH is "the LORD's anointed one": the king, whom the LORD chose by anointing (1 Samuel 24:6). The commonest view is Zedekiah, who fled the city, was caught on the plains of Jericho and taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4-7; Jeremiah 52:7-11). Josiah, whom Jeremiah lamented (2 Chronicles 35:25), was killed at Megiddo in 609 (2 Kings 23:29), not caught in a pit, but old tradition connects the two (the difficulty that Josiah could not have been caught in their pits is real): Rashi takes the anointed here to be Josiah, citing 2 Chronicles 35:25. Others see the Davidic king generally, as in Psalm 89:38-51. Jehoahaz and Jehoiachin, taken to Egypt and Babylon, are also described as trapped lions in Ezekiel 19. Christian readers have heard the verse as a picture of Christ's arrest, helped by the Greek and Latin wording "Christ the Lord". The Qumran scrolls 5Q6 and 5Q7 both preserve this verse; in both the word "anointed" is restored in the transcription, not visible. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew: it is a Davidic king's loss.

p: Zedekiah was caught on the plains of Jericho.
b: "Pits" is a hunter's word (see 3:53). Second Kings 25:4-7 and Jeremiah 39:4-7 tell how Zedekiah left the city by night through a gap in the wall, was caught, saw his sons killed, was blinded and taken to Babylon in bronze fetters.

p: Edom shared in the plunder, and the poet tells them their turn will come.
b: Edom, the nation descended from Esau, is accused of cheering Jerusalem's fall (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10-14; Ezekiel 25:12-14; 35). "Uz" is linked to Edom in Genesis 36:28 and in Jeremiah 25:20; Job lived "in the land of Uz" (Job 1:1), whose location is debated. The cup is the cup of God's anger (Jeremiah 25:15-29; 49:12; Obadiah 15-16), and to be "drunk" and naked is to be shamed (Habakkuk 2:15-16). The irony of "be glad" is the point: Edom is invited to celebrate before it drinks. In Jewish tradition Edom became a name for Rome and later for Christian Europe (Genesis Rabbah). These are later readings of the verse.

a: Your guilt is paid in full
p: Isaiah 40:2 says nearly the same of Zion.
b: Tam 'avonekh: "your guilt is complete", meaning the punishment for guilt has run its course. Isaiah 40:2 tells Jerusalem that her penalty has been paid. "He will not exile you again" is a promise; and yet chapter 5 follows, with the present troubles still going on. Different readers take this as the poet's hope, as an announcement of a past that has already ended, or as a faith that the poems do not yet see.

a: LORD, remember what has come over us
p: Chapter 5 has 22 verses like the alphabet poems, but no alphabet.
b: The 22 verses echo the number of letters, but the verses do not begin with the alphabet. Views: it is a deliberate dropping of the form because grief at last runs out of order; the number 22 is only a nod to the alphabet (commentators differ on which of these to prefer). The chapter is called a communal prayer: the verbs are "remember", "look", "see", "restore". The Plain English Translation does not call it an acrostic.

p: Foreigners, among them Edomites, settled in Judah's land.
b: The Hebrew nachalah is the family's ancestral land (Numbers 36:7-9). In the aftermath of 586 BC, neighbors moved into the empty south: Ezekiel 35:10 and 36:5 speak of Edom's claim on the land. After the fall, Jeremiah 39:10 says the Babylonians gave fields to the poor who were left. Both could be true in different places.

p: Assyria had fallen in 612-609 BC; the poem may name old powers.
b: To "give the hand" is to make a treaty or pledge. Hosea scolded Ephraim for running to Egypt and Assyria (Hosea 7:11; 12:1), and Jeremiah 2:18 says the same. By 586 Assyria was gone. Views: a reference to the past, when the kingdoms did seek their help; "Assyria" used for whatever power sits in Mesopotamia (compare Ezra 6:22, which calls the Persian king the king of Assyria); or a stock pairing. Egypt is where many refugees went after Gedaliah's murder (Jeremiah 43:1-7).

a: we are the ones who carry their guilt
t: Do children carry their parents' guilt?
p: The poem says both that our fathers sinned and that we sinned; Jews and Christians read the two verses differently.
b: The Law says God punishes the guilt of the fathers on the children (Exodus 20:5; 34:7), and also that fathers are not to be put to death for their children or the reverse (Deuteronomy 24:16; 2 Kings 14:6). Kings blames Manasseh's sins for the exile (2 Kings 23:26; Jeremiah 15:4). Jeremiah 31:29-30 and Ezekiel 18:2-4 reject the proverb about sour grapes: each dies for his own sin. And 5:16 says "we have sinned". Views: the generation is bearing real inherited consequence; the poem is quoting a proverb that Ezekiel will deny; the two verses together are both true, since the consequences fall on those who also share the sin. The Qumran scroll 5Q6 preserves 5:7 and agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling. For how Christians connect this to original sin, see the card.

p: The verb is the one used of Dinah and Tamar; in a conquered town the Plain English Translation says it plainly.
b: 'Innu is the piel of 'anah, "humble"; with a woman as object and a sexual setting it means to violate her sexually. It is the verb of Genesis 34:2 (Dinah), Judges 19:24 and 20:5 (the Levite's concubine), 2 Samuel 13:12-14, 22 and 32 (Amnon and Tamar) and Ezekiel 22:10-11. The shared term list renders it "dishonor" because the verb itself does not say force or consent, and the Plain English Translation keeps "dishonor" in those stories, where the narrator or a speaker says what was done. Here the verb stands alone in a list of things done to a defeated people, and the setting is conquest. Commentators take 5:11 to say that the women of Zion and the young women of Judah were raped, as Isaiah 13:16 and Zechariah 14:2 say of other conquered cities. The Plain English Translation says "raped" so that the verse is not softened. The Hebrew gives no subject, so the Plain English Translation uses a passive, as the Hebrew does. The book does not hide this and does not blame the women.
r: 2 Samuel 13:12; Genesis 34:2; Isaiah 13:16; Zechariah 14:2; Judges 19:24; Ezekiel 22:10

a: Princes were strung up by their hands
p: The Hebrew may mean they were hung up by their hands or hanged by the enemy's hand.
b: Beyadam is "by their hand". It can mean the princes were hung up by the hands as a torture, or that they were hanged "by the hand of" the enemy. Second Kings 25:21 and Jeremiah 52:10, 27 tell of nobles put to death at Riblah.

p: Grinding grain was women's work; for men it was slave labor.
b: Isaiah 47:2 tells Daughter Babylon to take the millstones and grind meal, the work of a slave woman. Samson ground at the mill in Gaza (Judges 16:21). The Greek of Swete's Codex Vaticanus reads here "chosen men took up weeping"; see the variant entry.

p: The poem confesses at the end, as it did at the start of the book.
b: In 1:5, 8, 14, 18, 20, 22; 3:39-42 the poem names its own sin. Here again the people say it. A book that has accused God of cruelty (2:1-8; 3:1-18) also admits guilt. It does not choose between them. Readers who take the book as only blaming the people, or as only protesting God, are each leaving out half of it.

p: Foxes or jackals in the ruins are the sign of a deserted site.
b: Shu'alim are foxes or jackals, animals that move into ruins (Nehemiah 4:3; Ezekiel 13:4). Micah 3:12 had said Zion would be plowed as a field and Jerusalem become heaps. Jeremiah 26:18 quotes the saying.

a: You, LORD, sit as king forever
p: The line is nearly Psalm 102:12; Psalm 102 is another prayer for Zion.
b: The confession of God's eternal kingship is close to Psalm 102:12 and to Psalm 9:7. Psalm 102 is the prayer of a sufferer who asks the LORD to arise and have compassion on Zion. The poet turns from the ruined throne of David to the throne that cannot be ruined.

a: Why do you keep forgetting us
p: Zion in Isaiah 49:14 says the same, and God answers.
b: Isaiah 49:14-16 gives Zion's words ("The LORD has forsaken me") and God's answer: a mother may forget her nursing child, yet he will not forget. Many readers hear Isaiah as the reply to this verse. Psalm 13:1, Psalm 44:23-24 and Psalm 74:1, 19 ask the same question of God.

a: Make our days new as in ancient times
p: In synagogue readings the verse is repeated after 5:22, so the book does not end on its last sentence.
b: The prayer "Bring us back to yourself, LORD, and we will come back" is close to Jeremiah 31:18 and Psalm 80:3, 7, 19; Hosea 14:2 has "return to the LORD". Who turns first? Here the people ask God to do the turning that 3:40 asked them to do. By Jewish custom, reported in the medieval Masoretic tradition and still followed, the reader repeats 5:21 after 5:22 so the book does not end on the word "rejected". The same is done at the end of Isaiah, Malachi and Ecclesiastes. The Latin church's Tenebrae reading ends differently, with a refrain not in the Hebrew: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, return to the LORD your God."

a: and your anger against us has gone too far
t: An ending that leaves the question open
p: The last verse is a question, a hope or a statement of fact.
b: Ki 'im ma'os ma'astanu can be read: "unless you have utterly rejected us" (the Plain English Translation: a bitter condition that the speakers refuse to believe); "for you have utterly rejected us" (the Greek and Latin: a statement); or as a question, "Have you utterly rejected us?". Jewish readers added the repeat of 5:21 so the book ends on hope. Linafelt in particular stresses the open ending: the book does not say whether God answered. See the variant entry.
